stem:
Gweru Door Makers is a fictional manufacturer of timber doors. It sells each door for US\$120 and makes 320 doors a month, which is 90 doors below its capacity. The owner, Mr Dube, is worried about cash because suppliers want to be paid in 30 days but customers take 60 days. He is considering two decisions: a school has offered to buy 60 doors at US\$90 each, and he wants to buy a new saw with a cash price of US\$9,000. The supplier offers hire purchase: a deposit of US\$1,800 and 24 monthly instalments of US\$360.

| Cost per door | US\$ |
| --- | ---: |
| Timber | 38 |
| Labour | 26 |
| Fittings | 11 |

| Monthly fixed cost | US\$ |
| --- | ---: |
| Factory rent | 2,350 |
| Supervisors' salaries | 2,950 |
| Insurance | 650 |

| Current items | US\$ |
| --- | ---: |
| Inventory (stock) | 21,500 |
| Trade receivables (debtors) | 12,800 |
| Cash | 1,450 |
| Trade payables (creditors) | 19,200 |
| Bank overdraft | 7,500 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Using the monthly figures for 320 doors, calculate:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the variable cost of making one door;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the monthly profit.
parts.explanation: Contribution per door = 120 - 75 = 45. Total contribution = 320 × 45 = 14,400. Profit = 14,400 - 5,950 = US\$8,450.
parts.workedSolution:
1. Contribution per door = 120 - 75 = US\$45.
2. Total contribution = 320 × 45 = US\$14,400.
3. Fixed costs = 2,350 + 2,950 + 650 = US\$5,950.
4. Profit = 14,400 - 5,950 = US\$8,450.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the extra profit from the school's order for 60 doors, assuming no new fixed costs and no effect on normal sales.
parts.explanation: Contribution per door = 90 - 75 = 15. Extra profit = 60 × 15 = US\$900.
parts.workedSolution:
1. Contribution per door on the order = 90 - 75 = US\$15.
2. Extra profit = 60 × 15 = US\$900.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Use the table of current items to:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: calculate the working capital;
parts.explanation: Current assets 35,750 - current liabilities 26,700 = US\$9,050.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: identify the statement that best explains Mr Dube's worry about cash.

options.content: Most of the current assets are inventory and receivables, not cash
options.rationale: Correct: only US\$1,450 of the US\$35,750 is cash, and suppliers are paid before customers.
Working capital is positive at US\$9,050.

options.content: Cash is the largest current asset
options.rationale: Cash is the smallest current asset.

parts.explanation: Working capital is positive, but cash is small and money is tied up in stock and receivables.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: For the new saw:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: calculate the total hire purchase price;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: calculate how much more this is than the cash price.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain two conditions that must hold for Mr Dube to accept the school's order at US\$90 a door.

points.description: The business must have spare capacity
Application: the factory can make 90 more doors and the order is for 60
The order must not reduce normal sales or force regular customers to expect lower prices
Application: other customers paying US\$120 must not hear of the US\$90 price and demand the same

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: There must be spare capacity: the factory can make 90 more doors and the school wants 60. The order must also not reduce normal sales or force regular customers to expect lower prices, because customers who pay US\$120 might demand the same price as the school.

parts.explanation: Two conditions, each applied.
hints: Think of capacity and of other customers.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Recommend how Mr Dube should finance the new saw, justifying your answer.

points.description: Hire purchase spreads the cost: only US\$1,800 is paid at the start
The total cost is US\$10,440, US\$1,440 more than paying cash
Cash is already short (only US\$1,450) and the overdraft is US\$7,500, so paying US\$9,000 cash is not possible
An extra bank loan would add to existing debt, which is already high
The saw will last for many years and hire purchase gives ownership at the end
Judgement with a reason: hire purchase, provided the instalments of US\$360 can be met from the extra profit

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Mr Dube should use hire purchase. It spreads the cost, so only US\$1,800 is paid at the start, which matters because he has only US\$1,450 in cash and an overdraft of US\$7,500. The total cost is US\$10,440, US\$1,440 more than the cash price, but the saw will last for many years and he will own it at the end. An extra bank loan would add to debt that is already high. He should choose hire purchase, provided the instalments of US\$360 can be met from the extra profit.

parts.explanation: Weighs cost, cash position and ownership to a recommendation.
hints: Use the cash and overdraft figures and the extra cost of hire purchase.

explanation: Variable cost US\$75; profit US\$8,450; special order US\$900; working capital US\$9,050; hire purchase US\$10,440; a recommendation on financing the saw.
hints: Contribution per door = price - variable cost.
Working capital = current assets - current liabilities.

stem:
Kwenda Safari Lodge is a fictional lodge near Hwange owned by two sisters, Thandeka and Sipho. The lodge has 14 rooms and employs 26 people. The sisters want to build a conference hall that will be rented out to companies and church groups, and must finish it before the dry season begins. The hall will cost US\$46,000. The sisters can pay US\$16,000 from the lodge's savings. A bank is willing to lend up to US\$22,000 at a fixed rate of interest, secured on the lodge, and a cousin who lives in Johannesburg has offered to join the business as a partner and put in the rest in return for a share of profit.

The building work has been planned as shown below.

| Activity | Description | Duration (days) | Follows |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| A | Prepare the site | 4 | none |
| B | Lay foundations | 6 | A |
| C | Order steel and roofing | 5 | none |
| D | Erect the frame | 7 | B, C |
| E | Roofing | 4 | D |
| F | Electrical work | 5 | D |
| G | Deliver furniture | 3 | C |
| H | Final fitting and inspection | 3 | E, F, G |

The sisters expect the hall to be hired for 140 delegate-days a month. Each delegate pays US\$48 a day; food and cleaning cost US\$20 for each delegate-day; the hall adds US\$2,800 a month to fixed costs. The lodge started the building project with US\$6,200 in the bank. The forecast for the first three months of the project is below.

| US\$ | Month 1 | Month 2 | Month 3 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Total receipts | 13,400 | 14,100 | 11,600 |
| Total payments | 14,900 | 16,700 | 14,000 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the minimum time in which the hall can be built.
parts.explanation: Forward pass: A 0-4, B 4-10, C 0-5, D 10-17 (after B at 10 and C at 5), E 17-21, F 17-22, G 5-8, H 22-25. Minimum duration = 25 days.
parts.workedSolution:
1. A finishes on day 4 and B on day 10; C finishes on day 5.
2. D waits for B (day 10) and C (day 5), so it runs from day 10 to day 17.
3. E (17-21), F (17-22) and G (5-8) lead into H, which starts at the latest finish, day 22.
4. H finishes on day 25: minimum duration 25 days.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Use the network to:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: identify the critical path;

options.rationale: This route takes 24 days, so it is not the longest.

parts.explanation: Only A, B, D, F, H takes the full 25 days.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: calculate the number of days by which roofing (E) can be delayed without delaying the hall.
parts.explanation: E can start on day 17 and must finish by day 22 (the start of H), so it has 22 - 21 = 1 day of spare time.
parts.workedSolution: 1. E can start on day 17 and must finish by day 22 (the start of H), so it has 22 - 21 = 1 day of spare time.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the monthly profit from the hall.
parts.explanation: Contribution per delegate-day = 48 - 20 = 28. Total contribution = 140 × 28 = 3,920. Profit = 3,920 - 2,800 = US\$1,120.
parts.workedSolution:
1. Contribution per delegate-day = 48 - 20 = US\$28.
2. Total contribution = 140 × 28 = US\$3,920.
3. Profit = 3,920 - 2,800 = US\$1,120.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the size of the overdraft at the end of month 3.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Analyse why the lodge may face cash flow problems during the building of the hall.

points.description: Payments for materials and labour are made before the hall earns anything
Application: payments exceed receipts in each of the three months
The balance falls from US\$6,200 to an overdraft of US\$300 by month 3
The hall's profit of US\$1,120 a month will take a long time to repay US\$46,000
Any delay on the critical path delays the first income while costs continue
A shortage of cash may stop work, delay the opening and lose bookings in the dry season

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Payments for materials and labour are made before the hall earns anything. In each of the three months payments exceed receipts, and the balance falls from US\$6,200 to an overdraft of US\$300. The hall's profit of US\$1,120 a month will take a long time to repay US\$46,000. Any delay on the critical path delays the first income while costs continue, and a shortage of cash may stop the work, delay the opening and lose bookings in the dry season.

parts.explanation: Each cause is linked to the figures in the case.
hints: Use the forecast figures and the critical path.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Evaluate how the sisters should finance the US\$46,000 hall, and recommend a course of action.

points.description: The savings of US\$16,000 carry no interest but would leave the lodge with little cash, and the forecast already shows an overdraft
The bank loan of US\$22,000 keeps ownership with the sisters, but interest is paid even in a slow month and the lodge is at risk if repayments are missed
The cousin would put in the remaining US\$8,000 with no interest, but would share the profit and some control
The profit of US\$1,120 a month is small compared with the loan repayments, so the sisters need to be sure of the bookings
Counter-argument: the hall adds to the lodge's income in the dry season and may bring guests to the rooms
Judgement with a reason: the loan plus savings, with a smaller share from the cousin only if the repayments cannot be met

levels.descriptor: Each source evaluated with figures from the case; risk and control weighed; a justified recommendation
Some sources evaluated with some application; recommendation weakly supported

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The savings of US\$16,000 carry no interest, but using them would leave the lodge with little cash and the forecast already shows an overdraft. The bank loan of US\$22,000 keeps ownership with the sisters, but interest must be paid even in a slow month and the lodge is at risk if repayments are missed. The cousin could put in the remaining US\$8,000 without interest, but would share the profit and some control. The hall's profit of US\$1,120 a month is small compared with the repayments, so the sisters must be sure of the bookings, although the hall may also bring extra guests to the rooms. The sisters should use the savings and the bank loan and bring in the cousin only if they cannot meet the repayments, as this keeps the ownership in the family.

parts.explanation: Weighs each source against the cash position and the profit from the hall.
hints: Use the profit from the hall and the overdraft in your answer.

explanation: Minimum duration 25 days; critical path A, B, D, F, H; profit US\$1,120 a month; overdraft US\$300; financing advice.
hints: Do a forward pass and take the larger finish where activities join.
Carry the closing balance forward each month.

stem: Essay. A growing business must decide where to find the money for expansion.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe four sources of finance that a medium-sized manufacturing business in Zimbabwe could use to expand. [10 marks]

points.description: Retained profit: profit kept in the business instead of being paid out
Development: no interest or repayment, but only available from past profit
Bank loan: a fixed sum repaid over a set period with interest
Development: usually needs security and interest must be paid whether or not profit is made
Share capital: selling shares to investors
Development: no repayment but dividends are paid and ownership is shared
Hire purchase or leasing: paying for equipment in instalments
Development: spreads the cost, but hire purchase costs more than the cash price
Link to expansion: the source must suit the amount and time period
An example from a Zimbabwean business, such as a bakery buying an oven

levels.descriptor: Four sources clearly described and developed, with a link to expansion and an example
Three or four sources described with some development

answerSpec.modelAnswer: A manufacturer could use retained profit, which is profit kept in the business instead of being paid out; it carries no interest or repayment, but it is available only from past profit. It could take a bank loan, a fixed sum repaid over a set period with interest; the bank usually wants security and the interest must be paid whether or not profit is made. A company could sell shares to investors, which needs no repayment but dividends are paid and ownership is shared. It could also buy equipment on hire purchase or lease it, which spreads the cost over instalments although hire purchase costs more than the cash price. For example, a bakery buying a new oven could use hire purchase to avoid a large payment at once. The source chosen must suit the amount needed and the time period.

parts.explanation: Four sources, each described and developed.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Discuss the factors that a business should consider when choosing between a bank loan and selling shares to raise finance for expansion. [15 marks]

points.description: The cost: a loan carries interest that must be paid, while shares carry dividends that can be varied
The risk: fixed interest must be paid even in a poor year, increasing the risk of failure
Existing debt: a business that already has high debt should be careful about borrowing more
Control: a loan leaves ownership unchanged, while shares share ownership and decisions
Security: a loan usually needs security such as property
Repayment: a loan must be repaid; share capital is permanent
Amount: shares can raise larger sums for a company
Form of business: only a company can sell shares, and only a public company to the public
Time and cost to arrange: a share issue is slower and costs more than a loan
Time period: a long-term need suits a long-term loan or shares, not an overdraft
Application: a family-owned firm that wants to keep control may prefer a loan
Application: a risky new venture with uncertain profit may prefer shares to reduce fixed payments
Interest rates: if rates are high or expected to rise, a loan is less attractive
Judgement: the best choice depends on how stable the profit is and how important control is
Reasoned conclusion linked to a named business

levels.descriptor: Several factors discussed and applied to a named business; both sources compared; a justified, qualified judgement
Several factors explained with some application; judgement weakly supported

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The first factor is cost. A bank loan carries interest, which must be paid whether or not the business makes a profit, whereas dividends on shares can be reduced in a poor year. This is linked to risk: a business with unstable profit, such as a clothing factory that depends on a few orders, may find fixed interest dangerous, particularly if it already has debt. Control is the next factor. A loan leaves ownership unchanged, so a family firm that wants to keep decisions in the family may prefer it, whereas shares bring new owners who share profit and may influence decisions. Security matters too: a bank usually wants property as security and may take it if repayments are missed, while share capital need not be repaid. The amount and form of business also matter. A company can raise large sums by selling shares, but a sole trader cannot sell shares at all, and only a public company can sell to the public. Shares take longer and cost more to arrange. The time period is also important: a long-term need such as a factory suits a loan over many years or share capital. Finally, high interest rates make a loan less attractive. The best choice depends on how stable the profit is and how important control is. A firm with steady orders and an owner who values control should usually borrow, while one with uncertain profit and a need for a large sum should consider shares.

parts.explanation: Weighs the main factors for each source and ends with a conditional judgement.

explanation: Describe four sources; discuss the factors in choosing between a loan and shares and conclude.
hints: In part (b) compare cost, risk and control for both sources.
Reach a judgement that depends on the business.

stem: Essay. Many manufacturers try to cut waste and improve quality at the same time.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe four techniques used in lean production. [10 marks]

points.description: Kaizen: continuous improvement through small changes suggested by workers
Development: many small gains reduce cost and defects over time
Quality circles: groups of workers who meet to solve quality problems
Development: they use workers' knowledge and raise motivation
Cell production: a small team makes a whole product or part
Development: faults are found sooner and workers take responsibility
Just-in-time: materials arrive only when needed
Development: less cash is tied up in stock but delivery must be reliable
Link to lean production: all aim to cut waste while keeping quality
An example from a Zimbabwean business, such as a garment factory in Bulawayo

levels.descriptor: Four techniques clearly described and developed, with a link to waste and an example
Three or four techniques described with some development

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Kaizen is continuous improvement, in which workers suggest small changes to the way the job is done; many small gains reduce cost and defects over time. Quality circles are groups of workers who meet to solve quality problems, using their knowledge of the job and raising motivation. Cell production organises a small team to make a whole product or part, so faults are found sooner and workers take responsibility for quality. Just-in-time delivers materials only when they are needed, so less cash is tied up in stock, although deliveries must be reliable. For example, a garment factory in Bulawayo could use cells to make whole shirts and JIT deliveries of cloth. All the techniques aim to cut waste while keeping quality.

parts.explanation: Four techniques, each described and developed.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Discuss whether a clothing factory in Zimbabwe should adopt lean production. [15 marks]

points.description: Lean production cuts waste, which lowers unit costs
Fewer defects improve quality and customer satisfaction
Less stock frees cash and storage space
Application: cloth is a large part of the cost, so cutting cloth stock would release cash
Workers' ideas (kaizen, quality circles) improve motivation and efficiency
Cell production makes workers multi-skilled and responsible
JIT depends on reliable suppliers; fuel or transport problems could stop production
Little spare capacity makes it hard to meet a sudden rise in orders
Training and reorganisation cost money before benefits arrive
Workers may resist change or fear job losses
Seasonal demand, such as school uniforms, makes forecasting harder
Counter-argument: parts of lean production, such as kaizen, carry little risk and can be introduced anyway
Appropriateness: steady orders, reliable suppliers and a stable workforce favour lean methods
Judgement: adopt lean methods in stages, with JIT only for materials with reliable supply
Reasoned conclusion linked to the factory

levels.descriptor: Benefits and risks weighed and applied to a clothing factory; appropriateness considered; a justified, qualified judgement
Benefits and risks explained with some application; judgement weakly supported

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Lean production could help a clothing factory. By cutting waste of cloth, time and defects it lowers unit costs, and fewer faulty garments improve quality. Cloth is a large part of the cost, so holding less of it would release cash and storage space, and kaizen and quality circles would use workers' ideas and raise motivation. Cell production would make workers multi-skilled and responsible for whole garments. However, there are risks. Just-in-time depends on reliable suppliers, and in Zimbabwe fuel or transport problems could stop production if there is no stock of cloth. Lean production also leaves little spare capacity, which makes it hard to meet a sudden rise in orders such as before the school year. Training and reorganising the factory cost money before the benefits arrive, and some workers may resist change or fear job losses. Kaizen and quality circles carry little risk and can be introduced anyway. Lean methods suit a factory with steady orders, reliable suppliers and a stable workforce. The factory should adopt lean production in stages, starting with kaizen and cells, and use just-in-time only for materials whose supply is reliable.

parts.explanation: Weighs benefits and risks for a clothing factory and ends with a staged judgement.

explanation: Describe four techniques; discuss whether a clothing factory should adopt lean production and conclude.
hints: In part (b) weigh benefits against supplier and demand risks.
Reach a judgement that depends on the factory's conditions.
